references.excerpt: Patient positioning is a shared responsibility between the surgical and anaesthetic teams. The anaesthetist retains particular responsibility for protection of pressure points, the eyes, peripheral nerves, the airway and haemodynamics during and after every position change. Joints should be kept in mid-range; eyes lubricated and taped; padded supports used at vulnerable nerves (ulnar, common fibular, brachial plexus); arms abducted no more than 90°; and steep head-down positions limited where possible because of the risks of raised intra-ocular and intracranial pressure, facial and airway oedema, and the patient slipping.

cards.question: What are the physiological consequences of steep Trendelenburg?
cards.answer: Increased ICP and IOP, cephalad shift of diaphragm with reduced FRC and atelectasis, increased airway pressures, facial and laryngeal oedema, conjunctival oedema, and increased risk of regurgitation. Cardiovascular: increased preload but reduced cardiac output if prolonged. Mitigate with limited tilt time, PEEP, and lung-protective ventilation.

cards.question: Which nerves are most commonly injured by intraoperative positioning?
cards.answer: Ulnar nerve at the elbow (commonest — supine, arms tucked or abducted >90°), brachial plexus (shoulder abduction >90° or shoulder braces in Trendelenburg), common peroneal at the fibular head (lithotomy/lateral), and sciatic (sitting position). ASA Closed Claims show ulnar and brachial plexus injuries account for ~70 % of positioning claims.

cards.question: How is perioperative visual loss prevented in prone surgery?
cards.answer: Avoid direct pressure on the globe (use Mayfield pins or a free-floating headrest with mirror check every 20 min), maintain head above heart, keep haematocrit >25 %, avoid prolonged hypotension, limit crystalloid, and consider staging cases predicted to exceed 6 h. ASA Practice Advisory on POVL (2019) recommends informed consent for high-risk prone spinal surgery.
